title: The scheme and its gates
paras: Let's start with the scheme and its gates. Schedule 2, Part 1 of the G-P-D-O grants planning permission nationally for works within the curtilage of a dwellinghouse, and there are nine classes to know. Class A covers extensions and alterations. Class A-A, additional storeys. Classes B and C, roof enlargements and other roof alterations. Class D is porches, Class E outbuildings, Class F hard surfaces, Class G chimneys and flues, and Class H microwave antennae. Now, most domestic building work in England goes ahead under these rights rather than by application — which is exactly why they repay a careful read before anyone orders materials.

Three gates apply before you open any class. First, Part 1 serves dwellinghouses only. Flats and maisonettes get no householder rights, and neither does a house divided into flats. Second, a dwelling that exists only by virtue of a Part 3 change-of-use right — that's Classes G, M, M-A, N, P, P-A or Q — is expressly excluded from the whole of Part 1. So the barn converted under Class Q, and the office converted under Class M-A, have no householder rights at all. No extensions, no outbuildings, no porch. And third, the use has to actually be as a dwellinghouse. The rights attach to the use, not the bricks.

Every principal allowance is measured against the original dwellinghouse — the house as first built, or as it stood on the 1st of July 1948 if it's older than that. Anything added since then counts against the allowance today, whoever built it, with or without permission. So a rear addition from the nineteen-seventies can leave a present-day owner with no Class A headroom at all — and here's the catch: neither the estate agent nor the deeds will say so.

Article 2(3) land — conservation areas, National Parks, the Broads, National Landscapes and World Heritage Sites — carries tighter rules throughout the Part. Under Class A alone, it strips out cladding, side extensions and multi-storey rear extensions. And Class B, the dormer class, is excluded on such land entirely. Separately, rights can be removed on any land by an article 4 direction, or by a condition on an existing permission — and modern estate permissions remove them as a matter of routine.

So the working sequence is fixed. Establish that the building is a house, and how it came to be one. Work out what the original house looked like. Work out what land it stands on. Check whether anything has removed the rights. And find out what's already been built. Only then do you open the class and start measuring.

title: Class A: extensions day to day
paras: Now to Class A — extensions, day to day. Class A permits the enlargement, improvement or other alteration of a dwellinghouse, and this is where you'll find the arithmetic most people mean by permitted development. A single-storey rear extension may go four metres beyond the original rear wall of a detached house, or three metres in any other case, to a maximum height of four metres. And where any part of it comes within two metres of any boundary of the curtilage, the eaves can't exceed three metres.

Go more than one storey and it tightens. You can't extend beyond the original rear wall by more than three metres, you need at least seven metres from the rear boundary, and the roof pitch has to match the existing house so far as practicable. Upper floors also bring the neighbour-facing conditions into play. Any upper-floor window in a side elevation has to be obscure-glazed and non-opening — unless the opening parts sit more than one point seven metres above the floor of the room.

Side extensions are permitted as a single storey only, to a maximum height of four metres, and no wider than half the width of the original dwellinghouse. On article 2(3) land there's no side extension right at all. No multi-storey rear extension either. And no exterior cladding in stone, artificial stone, pebble dash, render, timber, plastic or tiles.

The general limits sit over everything. Nothing forward of the principal elevation where it fronts a highway. Nothing higher than the highest part of the existing roof. Eaves no higher than the existing eaves. Total coverage by buildings within the curtilage is capped at fifty per cent, excluding the original house. And no verandas, balconies or raised platforms — and a platform counts as raised once it exceeds thirty centimetres. Materials have to be of similar appearance to the existing house — except for conservatories.

In practice, measurement discipline decides these cases. Heights are taken from the highest part of the adjacent natural ground. Depth runs from the original rear wall — not the current one. And a wraparound extension has to satisfy the side limits and the rear limits at the same time, which, in practice, it rarely can. Where the built dimensions exceed the limits by any margin, the whole extension is unauthorised. Remember, Part 1 has no concept of a minor breach.

title: The larger home extension route
paras: Next, the larger home extension route. Paragraph A one, sub-paragraph G, doubles the single-storey rear allowance — to eight metres for a detached house, and six metres for any other — through the neighbour consultation scheme. Think of it as prior notification with teeth. The right only exists if you follow the process to the letter, and the enlarged allowance isn't available on article 2(3) land, or for anything other than a single-storey rear extension.

The developer submits a written description stating the depth beyond the original rear wall, the maximum height, and the eaves height — along with a site plan and the addresses of adjoining premises. The authority then notifies adjoining owners and occupiers, who have twenty-one days to object. If any adjoining neighbour does object, the authority must assess the effect on the amenity of adjoining premises — and only that — and grant or refuse prior approval accordingly.

Work may begin on one of three events, and only these. First, written notice that prior approval is not required. Second, written notice granting prior approval. Or third, the expiry of forty-two days from the authority receiving the notification, without any decision. So silence after forty-two days is a lawful start — which is unusual among prior approval regimes, and widely disbelieved by clients and authorities alike.

The development has to be built in accordance with the details submitted, or as approved, and the stated dimensions are the enforceable envelope. The assessment, where it's triggered, is confined to adjoining amenity. Design, character and highway objections get no purchase within this scheme — however firmly they're made.

title: Roofs: Classes B and C
paras: On to the roof — Classes B and C. Class B permits the enlargement of the roof: dormers and hip-to-gable conversions. It works within a cubic content allowance — forty cubic metres for a terrace house, fifty cubic metres for any other, measured externally. And here's the thing: the allowance is cumulative. Any previous enlargement of the roof, by any owner at any time, counts against it. And Class B isn't available on article 2(3) land at all.

The enlargement mustn't exceed the highest part of the existing roof, and mustn't extend beyond the plane of the existing roof slope on the principal elevation where it fronts a highway. Other than hip-to-gable works, it has to be set back at least twenty centimetres from the original eaves, measured along the roof slope. Materials must be of similar appearance. Side-facing windows carry the obscure-glazed, non-opening condition. And no veranda, balcony or raised platform may be formed.

Class C covers roof alterations that don't enlarge — rooflights being the everyday case. The alteration can't project more than fifteen centimetres beyond the plane of the roof slope, and can't rise above the highest part of the roof. Now, Class C survives on article 2(3) land — which is exactly why rooflights stay feasible in conservation areas when dormers are not.

Where the ambition is a whole extra floor rather than a dormer, the choice lies between Class B arithmetic and Class A-A, additional storeys. Different gates, different processes, different politics. The dormer is measured in cubic metres and self-assessed. The storey goes through prior approval, with the authority holding a view on external appearance. So run both calculations before you choose a route.

title: Class AA: additional storeys
paras: Which brings us to Class A-A — additional storeys. Class A-A, inserted in August 2020, permits up to two additional storeys on a house of two or more storeys, or one additional storey on a single-storey house — subject to gates that exclude much of the stock. The house must have been constructed between the 1st of July 1948 and the 28th of October 2018. It mustn't exceed eighteen metres in total height once extended. And the right doesn't apply on article 2(3) land, or to houses created by the Part 3 change-of-use rights.

Unlike the rest of Part 1, nothing happens without prior approval here. The application is assessed on a long statutory list — including the external appearance of the dwelling, the impact on the amenity of neighbouring premises, and air traffic and defence considerations where relevant. So the authority effectively holds a design judgment over the proposal, and refusals on appearance are routine.

And the conditions carry on after the build. The developer must notify the authority on completion of the development — a duty unique in Part 1, and easily missed. The class also cross-refers to the National Planning Policy Framework by its publication date. S-I 2026 number 313 updated those references to the December 2024 Framework in April 2026 — and they'll fall out of date again the moment a new Framework publishes. So read the class against the current amendment position, always.

And there's no government technical guidance on Class A-A at all. The 2019 householder guidance predates it, and has never been revised. So your only authoritative sources are the Order itself, and the accumulating appeal decisions.

title: Outbuildings and surfaces: E and F
paras: Now, outbuildings and surfaces — Classes E and F. Class E permits buildings, enclosures, pools and containers required for a purpose incidental to the enjoyment of the dwellinghouse as such. The garden office, the gym, the workshop, the swimming pool. Incidental is the load-bearing word here. Primary living accommodation is not incidental — so an outbuilding providing a bedroom, or working as a self-contained annexe, falls outside the class, whatever it's labelled on the drawings.

The limits run like this. Single storey only. Maximum height four metres with a dual-pitched roof, three metres otherwise — and two and a half metres for any part within two metres of a curtilage boundary. Eaves capped at two and a half metres throughout. Nothing forward of the principal elevation. And the same fifty per cent curtilage coverage cap it shares with extensions — so the existing shed and the new garden room count together. Further restrictions apply on article 2(3) land, and in National Parks, the Broads and National Landscapes, where siting and size limits tighten. So check paragraph E one before you fix a position.

Raised platforms above thirty centimetres are excluded here too, just as in Class A — which catches decking — and an outbuilding may not contain a microwave antenna. The use limit persists after construction, as well. A building erected lawfully as a store becomes unlawful the moment it becomes a dwelling, and the change is enforceable as a material change of use.

Class F permits hard surfaces incidental to the enjoyment of the dwellinghouse. The single operative condition bites at the front. Where a new or replacement surface between the principal elevation and a highway exceeds five square metres, it must either be made of porous materials, or drain to a permeable area within the curtilage. The rule exists for surface-water flooding — and, tellingly, it's enforced most often after the flood.

title: Porches, chimneys, antennae — and proving it
paras: Finally — porches, chimneys, antennae, and proving it. The small classes round out the domestic set. Class D permits a porch outside any external door: a maximum of three square metres of ground area, measured externally, a maximum height of three metres, and no part within two metres of any boundary with a highway. Class G permits chimneys, flues and soil pipes, provided they don't rise one metre or more above the highest part of the roof — with siting restrictions on designated land. And Class H permits up to two microwave antennae, subject to size limits — broadly one metre, with only one antenna over sixty centimetres — a cubic capacity cap of thirty-five litres, chimney-mounting rules, and visibility restrictions on article 2(3) land. The conditions require siting to minimise visual impact, and removal once the antenna is no longer needed.

Then comes the part every simplified guide leaves out. Permitted development is self-assessed. No one checks the measurements, no one issues anything, and the owner's confidence is not a legal status. The only instrument that certifies lawfulness is a certificate under the 1990 Act — section 192 for proposed works, section 191 for works done — determined on the balance of probabilities, against evidence.

That certificate discipline really matters at sale. Purchasers' solicitors increasingly ask for proof that unconsented works were lawful, and a file of dated drawings, measurements and photographs — or better, a certificate — answers in a way recollection simply cannot. Where any dimension sits near a limit, the section 192 certificate before the build is the cheap insurance. The section 191 after a dispute is the expensive kind.

And one last thing — the boundary of the subject. Part 1 answers the planning question only. Building regulations approval, the Party Wall etc. Act, private covenants, drainage easements and protected species law all apply on their own terms — and none of them has read the G-P-D-O. The lawful extension that breaches a covenant is still a breach of covenant.
